ent_method_design_for_manufacturing.name: Design for Manufacturing (DFM)
ent_method_design_for_manufacturing.summary: An engineering practice of designing parts and assemblies so that they are easy, repeatable, and cost-effective to manufacture at scale.
ent_method_design_for_manufacturing.body:
## Overview

Design for Manufacturing (DFM) is an engineering design approach that makes parts and assemblies easy, repeatable, and economical to manufacture at scale. What it truly changes is not how individual parts are processed, but the entire decision-making chain from product concept to mass production—holding design teams accountable for mold costs, yield, and cycle time before drawings are frozen.

ent_method_design_for_assembly.name: Design for Assembly (DFA)
ent_method_design_for_assembly.summary: A design methodology that reduces part count, simplifies joining, and shortens assembly time to lower production cost and improve reliability.
ent_method_design_for_assembly.body:
## Overview

Design for Assembly (DFA) is an engineering design method that reduces production costs and improves reliability by decreasing part count, simplifying connection methods, and shortening assembly time. What it truly changes is not the manufacturing precision of individual parts, but the systemic economics and maintainability of the entire product from design to mass production.

## Content

### What It Is: Precise Definition

Design for Assembly (DFA) belongs to the **method** type, within the field of manufacturing processes, positioned at the upstream value chain level. Its core definition is: **a design method that reduces part count, simplifies connection methods, shortens assembly time, thereby lowering production costs and improving reliability**. ent_method_supplier_qualification.name: Supplier Qualification
ent_method_supplier_qualification.summary: Process of auditing and approving component manufacturers for quality, capacity, traceability, and compliance before mass production.
ent_method_supplier_qualification.body:
## Overview
Supplier Qualification is the process of auditing and approving component manufacturers for quality, capacity, traceability, and compliance before mass production. What it truly changes is not the one-time decision of "which supplier to choose," but rather a systematic risk management framework for "whether the supplier can consistently and reliably deliver qualified parts." In the humanoid robotics field, this process covers all critical components, from harmonic reducers to torque sensors, and serves as a mandatory gateway connecting design validation with mass production.

ent_paper_kawaharazuka_mevius2_practical.name: MEVIUS2: Practical Open-Source Quadruped Robot with Sheet Metal Welding and Multimodal Perception
ent_paper_kawaharazuka_mevius2_practical.name_en: MEVIUS2: Practical Open-Source Quadruped Robot with Sheet Metal Welding and Multimodal Perception
ent_paper_kawaharazuka_mevius2_practical.summary: Kawaharazuka et al. present MEVIUS2, a Spot-sized open-source quadruped robot built primarily with sheet-metal-welded and machined aluminum components that can all be procured through e-commerce, and validate its rough-terrain locomotion and LiDAR/HDR-camera perception capabilities.
ent_paper_kawaharazuka_mevius2_practical.body:
## Overview
Various quadruped robots have been developed to date, and thanks to reinforcement learning, they are now capable of traversing diverse types of rough terrain. In parallel, there is a growing trend of releasing these robot designs as open-source, enabling researchers to freely build and modify robots themselves. However, most existing open-source quadruped robots have been designed with 3D printing in mind, resulting in structurally fragile systems that do not scale well in size, leading to the construction of relatively small robots. Although a few open-source quadruped robots constructed with metal components exist, they still tend to be small in size and lack multimodal sensors for perception, making them less practical. ent_paper_guidetti_stress_flow_guided_no.name: Stress Flow Guided Non-Planar Print Trajectory Optimization for Additive Manufacturing of Anisotropic Polymers
ent_paper_guidetti_stress_flow_guided_no.name_en: Stress Flow Guided Non-Planar Print Trajectory Optimization for Additive Manufacturing of Anisotropic Polymers
ent_paper_guidetti_stress_flow_guided_no.summary: Presents a trajectory optimization framework that aligns non-planar fused filament fabrication paths with principal stress flow, demonstrating up to 44x failure strength and 6x stiffness improvements on a 5-axis printer using liquid crystal polymer.
ent_paper_guidetti_stress_flow_guided_no.body:
## Overview
When manufacturing parts using material extrusion additive manufacturing and anisotropic polymers, the mechanical properties of a manufactured component are strongly dependent on the print trajectory orientation. We conduct non-planar slicing and optimize the print trajectories to maximize the alignment between the material deposition direction and the stress flow induced by a predefined load case. The trajectory optimization framework considers manufacturability constraints in the form of uniform layer height and line spacing. We demonstrate the method by manufacturing a load bearing mechanical bracket using a 5-axis 3D printer and a liquid crystal polymer material. ent_paper_santos_a_robotic_system_to_aut.name: A Robotic System to Automate the Disassembly of PCB Components
ent_paper_santos_a_robotic_system_to_aut.name_en: A Robotic System to Automate the Disassembly of PCB Components
ent_paper_santos_a_robotic_system_to_aut.summary: Santos, Marques, and Neto present a robotic system that automates desoldering and extraction of PCB components from e-waste using a customized tool on a collaborative robot arm with Cartesian force control, reporting approximately 100% desoldering success for larger components.
ent_paper_santos_a_robotic_system_to_aut.body:
## Overview
The disposal and recycling of electronic waste (e-waste) is a global challenge. The disassembly of components is a crucial step towards an efficient recycling process, avoiding the destructive methods. Although most disassembly work is still done manually due to the diversity and complexity of components, there is a growing interest in developing automated methods to improve efficiency and reduce labor costs. This study aims to robotize the desoldering process and extracting components from printed circuit boards (PCBs), with the goal of automating the process as much as possible. ent_paper_bill_of_materials_2024.name: Bill of Materials
ent_paper_bill_of_materials_2024.summary: Structured list of all parts, subassemblies, and raw materials required to build one humanoid robot unit.
ent_paper_bill_of_materials_2024.body:
## Overview

A Bill of Materials (BOM) is the most fundamental document describing a product's composition, listing all raw materials, components, subassemblies, and their quantity relationships required to manufacture one product. In the humanoid robot domain, the BOM is not only the starting point for cost accounting but also the core data structure for procurement, planning, inventory management, and supplier collaboration. What it truly changes is not document management, but rather the transformation of an entire complex machine's physical composition into a quantifiable, optimizable, and negotiable strategic asset.

ent_process_cnc_machining.name: CNC Precision Machining
ent_process_cnc_machining.summary: Computer-numerical-control machining processes that produce high-precision structural parts such as joint housings, brackets, and shafts to tight tolerances.
ent_process_cnc_machining.body:
## Overview

CNC precision machining is a manufacturing technology that uses computer numerical control systems to govern the relative motion between cutting tools and workpieces, removing material from metal or non-metal materials to shape parts. In the field of humanoid robotics, what it truly changes is not how parts are machined, but the trade-off logic among "design freedom—batch size—cost"—enabling engineers to take responsibility for the manufacturability of every feature before the drawing is finalized.
